source.title: From Latent Space to Jacobian Space: Measuring, Evading, and Training Against Safety-Content Accessibility

page_placements.theme: Compression: quantization mechanism, precision changes and pruning

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some tables and figures are flattened in the extraction, and §4.8 contains an apparent garbled correlation value ('r = −−').
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies J-space safety recognition, monitor evasion, and quantization, and cites unlearning work, but it does not test recovery of targeted knowledge after unlearning as defined by versions A–F.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a quantized abliterated-model result, but its SafetyAUC measures danger-prompt versus safe-prompt separability, not targeted-knowledge performance or recovery. The J-space attack results concern evading a monitor, not recovering unlearned knowledge. Other J-space results are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper measures J-space danger-recognition separability (SafetyAUC), DPO effects and GCG evasion of a J-space monitor. It applies no unlearning method and measures no targeted-knowledge accuracy or its recovery. WMDP and unlearning-durability work are cited only in related work. The abliterated-model NF4 result concerns removal of a refusal direction, not unlearning, and its metric is prompt separability, not knowledge.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that ordinary DPO can install refusal while J-space recognition falls to chance (0.5B), and that GCG-style suffixes evade a prompt-side J-space monitor at every scale; only a learned monitor rung resists its adaptive re-attack. They conclude that safety monitoring and training must operate on accessibility, not on outputs alone.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not apply an unlearning recipe from the claim; it measures J-space recognition in abliterated and other checkpoints under different inference regimes.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity of its J-space metrics to lens-fit seed, calibration corpus, readout depth, target window, lexicon, and inference precision/quantization. These are not tests of the claim's recovery attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Qwen3-1.7B-abliterated: J-space SafetyAUC is 0.293±0.041 in bf16 and 0.392 under NF4. The base model scores 0.798 in bf16 and 0.817 under NF4. The authors call this partial NF4 recovery of recognition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: 4-bit quantization can partly restore J-space danger recognition in a refusal-abliterated model. This is a recognition analogue of quantization recovery, not knowledge recovery after unlearning.

record.problems: For the claim at issue, the paper does not evaluate targeted-knowledge behavior or unlearning-recovery attacks. The directly adjacent abliterated-model quantization finding uses J-space SafetyAUC instead; the NF4 entry has no uncertainty value stated in Table 10.
record.rows_left_out: Other J-space recognition, DPO, monitor-evasion, steering, and quantization results were left out because they do not measure recovery of targeted knowledge after unlearning.

untested.parts: No unlearning method, no targeted-knowledge accuracy, no general-ability check.
No fine-tuning relearning after unlearning. The DPO here is safety tuning of base models, not relearning.
Abliteration and steering along a refusal or safety direction are studied, but not restoration of unlearned knowledge.
NF4 quantization of an abliterated checkpoint shifts SafetyAUC. No unlearned weights and no knowledge recovery are measured.
GCG suffixes jailbreak refusal-tuned models, but no unlearned knowledge is probed.

record.verdict_notes: The record's classification holds. All four rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The abliteration and quantization result is adjacent to version D but uses a different construct (refusal-direction removal, prompt separability) and is correctly kept in fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Unlearning effects on targeted-knowledge accuracy, general ability, and recovery attacks.
Fine-tuning recovery from unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples after unlearning.
Restoration of targeted knowledge by activation-direction ablation, or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting that knowledge.
Recovery of targeted-knowledge behavior after quantizing unlearned weights. The paper measures J-space danger recognition in an abliterated checkpoint instead.
Recovery of targeted knowledge by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information after unlearning.
A counter-method tested for resistance to the claim's unlearning-recovery attacks.

relation.reason: Unlearning work (WMDP, Rosati et al., Łucki et al.) is cited only in related work, line 191. The abliterated/NF4 result is about refusal-direction removal and recognition, not unlearning.

tranche.reason: The paper measures J-space danger recognition (SafetyAUC), DPO effects and GCG evasion. It applies no unlearning method and measures no targeted-knowledge accuracy. WMDP (Li et al. 2024) and Łucki et al. 2024 appear only in related work.

source_check.notes: Table 10's layout is garbled, but its columns map cleanly. GPU columns use seeds {10, 11}. The abliterated row is a replication on a public huihui-ai checkpoint run on a capable GPU. The text does not say whether 'Qwen3-1.7B base' is the pretrained base or the abliterated model's parent. NF4 shifts other models' SafetyAUC both up and down (135M tuned 0.581->0.665; 0.5B tuned 0.564->0.430), so the abliterated +0.099 is not unique to that model.

statements.correction: Abliterated Qwen3-1.7B: SafetyAUC 0.293±0.041 (bf16/GPU), 0.392 (NF4/GPU). Qwen3-1.7B base: 0.798±0.048 (bf16/GPU), 0.817 (NF4/GPU). The authors describe partial NF4 recovery of recognition.
statements.problem: Numbers match Table 10. The authors call the NF4 result 'partial NF4 recovery', but it stays below chance (0.392 < 0.5). The measure is danger-recognition SafetyAUC on an abliterated model, not targeted-knowledge accuracy after unlearning.
